How Apocalypter builds its terrain, places encounters, remembers discoveries, and decides what survives the journey back.

Installed Windows gameUnity 2020.3.49f1 · MapMagic 2.1.12Source-backed review

Quick answers to the gameplay questions

What happens when I travel more than 5 km away from a camp?

The game destroys ordinary registered dynamic items and cars beyond 5,000 m during its distance cleanup. Enemies, critters, merchant NPCs and physical merchandise commonly belong to that item list. This cleanup does not reset the camp’s spawn flags. If the camp shell is retained, returning can find those categories empty: the camp remembers that it already spawned them.

This is conditional on object identity and loading. Terrain streaming can retain, recycle or create a shell; save/load can restore some shell flags. There is no universal “return after X days” replenishment rule in the reviewed spawners.

Question Answer from this build
Can the same kind of camp appear again after discovery? Yes. The codex records a discovered type. Seeded placement can produce many instances of that type.
Does visiting a camp prevent all later camps of that type? No. Individual map visits, local spawn completion and type discovery are different records.
Does killing the enemies reset a camp? No reset path was found in its usual one-shot spawners. Individual batches finish with OnOff = 1.
Can a named boss appear again? Another site of its archetype can exist. Its initial spawn check suppresses the boss after the corresponding saved death flag becomes true. An already armed spawner has an important exception, explained below.
Is 5 km a respawn threshold? No. It is a dynamic-object destruction threshold. Terrain visibility uses tile indices, and spawn state uses separate flags.
Does saving refresh what merchants want? A nearby merchant’s static wanted-list FSM has no native save-triggered refresh path. A fresh load/recreated site generates its unsaved wanted list again. Saving can activate inactive dynamic items, which is a different side effect.
Is the whole map stored in the save? The save retains the graph seed/world offset, registered dynamic objects, progression and selected variables. Terrain is regenerated from the recipe.

This is a design document for the observed implementation, assembled from the installed game’s Unity scene/prefab assets and decompiled framework code. It is not an intended-design proposal. “POI” means the static camp, cave, building or wreck shell. The user’s “POE” is treated as an encounter/site term: no separate POE selection subsystem was identified in the inspected world graph. Confidence is strongest for explicit fields and state transitions; route-specific pool reuse and event timing remain runtime-dependent.

Sources: persistence review, encounter review, terrain review. Complete serialized spawner definitions appear in the evidence appendix.

The architecture: five interacting layers

World generation is split between a deterministic terrain graph and runtime PlayMaker state machines. A landmark’s shape, its current occupants and its remembered history are not one object with one lifetime.

Seed + world coordinate
MapMagic recipe→Terrain + road fields
Generated surfaces→Camp/cave/building/wreck
Static shell→Local trigger + random roll
Dynamic population→Flags + object snapshots
Saved state
Layer Main owner What it decides What it does not guarantee
Geography MapMagicObject + MyDesert graph Heights, texture masks, roads, candidate positions, shell variant Identical runtime loot or enemy batches
Static POI shell Objects output/pool Camp meshes, buildings, spawn volumes, markers and local FSMs Permanent object identity at a coordinate
Local population Child ItemSpawner FSMs Batch count, weighted prefab choice, creation, registration and completion Automatic restocking after death/destruction
History/progression Codex, map-icon Visited, global Boss_* flags Discovered types, individual marker visits, boss defeats A single universal “camp cleared” state
Persistence/cleanup NewGO_ArrayList, save coordinator, cleanup FSMs Save objects and selected variables; sleep or destroy far objects Resetting the source spawner when an object is deleted

MapMagic’s coordinate noise is deterministic for the root seed, subnode seed and world coordinate. Runtime spawners use Unity’s gameplay random stream. Therefore, the same seed can reliably reconstruct the same site type at the same transform while its first-run loot, condition and NPC choices differ. Loaded objects and restored flags can override that first-run behavior.

The graph does not ask whether Camp_10 has been discovered, whether a boss has been killed, or how many road kilometres have been driven before selecting a shell. Those are runtime systems downstream of placement. Some repository mods add progression-based ambushes; those rules should not be attributed to vanilla geography.

Sources: terrain review, Graph serializer and Noise implementation; encounter and persistence reviews, decoded child FSMs.

Terrain generation, textures and the starting area

The actual terrain configuration

New games use the seed entered in the title menu. The input defaults to 12345, accepts integer input with a nine-character limit, and is read continuously by GetSeed. Clicking New Game copies that value into the newly loaded SaveLoadGame.seed, which is applied to Graph.random.Seed before terrain generation. No random-seed action was found among the 37 inspected menu FSMs. Empty/invalid text follows the input action's int.TryParse fallback to zero rather than choosing a random world. Loading a save restores its saved root seed instead.

The installed scene uses 5,000 × 5,000 m tiles. The full terrain heightmap is 1025 samples per side, giving 1024 intervals at 4.8828125 m spacing. Its draft is 65 samples per side, or 78.125 m spacing. The configured vertical range is 600 m. Full generation includes 16 border samples; drafts include two. Height edges weld over five samples and splat edges over two.

The camera drives infinite tile generation. Full terrain and its POI objects are active within mainRange = 1, normally a 3 × 3 tile neighbourhood. Draft generation uses generateRange = 2, a 5 × 5 neighbourhood. An extra retention margin keeps already existing tiles to reduce churn. Tile (0,0) is pinned. The scene processes generated objects in batches of 500 and sets a 3 ms apply budget; these describe scheduling, not a guarantee that generation completes within 3 ms.

How the height field is built

The base height chain is:

Perlin noise → height curve → terraces → erosion → levels
Stage Actual authored values Effect
Noise Perlin; node seed 12345; size 5127 m; intensity 1.13; detail 0.45; turbulence 0; offset (0,0) Broad seeded variation, evaluated in world coordinates
Curve Six remap points: (0,0), (0.39568,0.15108), (0.64748,0.46763), (0.74820,0.87770), (0.86331,0.96403), (1,1) Remaps the noise into lower stretches and steeper high areas
Terrace Eight levels; uniformity 0.25; steepness 0.36; node seed 12345 Creates stepped elevation structure
Erosion Three iterations; durability 0.62; erosion 1; sediment 0.45; fluidity five; relax zero Redistributes height and sediment; drafts reduce iteration work
Levels Input 0.11–0.991; gamma 1.307; output 0–1 Normalizes/remaps the eroded field

Native plugin code performs the underlying noise and erosion calculations. The managed code and assets establish the operation order and parameters; they do not expose every native numerical step.

Road corridors and site pads then modify this base, in a specific dependency order:

base height
  → small road stamp → small site pads
  → large road stamp → large site pads
  → desert wreck pads → dry wreck/cave pads → main cave pads
  → final HeightOutput

This matters because later sites sample and flatten an already modified terrain field. They are not all independently placed on untouched noise.

Terrain appearance and the meaning of “biome”

MyDesert has one terrain graph with 140 enabled nodes. It does not contain a Whittaker climate selector or a separate BiomesSet graph. Its desert/dry/cliff labels describe texture masks derived from height, slope and cavity.

Texture layer Input
Desert Background layer
dry Convex cavity, intensity 20, spread 100, from the small-road/small-pad height field
redDesert Height contrast: brightness 0, contrast 3
stone_ground Concave cavity, intensity 5, spread 20
Cliff Slope 25–90°, transition range 30°
road / road2 The two road spline strokes
building / building2 Small/large site-ground strokes, radius 20 m / 70 m

Layers blend in authored order and finalize into normalized splat channels. The later road and building masks influence what appears on top. The generated dry texture product also feeds vegetation and POI probability masks, so visual terrain and placement are related.

Two named matrix nodes, DryGrassyMask and DesertMask, have their third mask input unconnected. The actual implementation returns input A, the dry field, in that situation. Their opposing invert settings do not create independent climate maps. Similarly, the sandstorm placement stream has a Slide node with no height input, so that node passes points through. These are concrete graph wiring details that matter more than editor labels.

The fixed starting area

The authored start coordinate is (1696, 0, 2533) in MapMagic world space. A StartPos terrain lock has a 12 m radius and 6 m transition. Its relative-height behavior preserves the starter patch’s form while adapting its height during regeneration.

The start point is combined with the small-camp candidates for road linking and ground treatment. It is not added to the random Camp ObjectsOutput stream. Consequently, connecting the home/start area to roads does not mean the graph randomly chooses an extra camp at that coordinate.

Source: terrain review, scene MapMagicObject path ID 11687, graph path ID 103111, and complete graph topology.

How POI positions and variants are selected

Position generation happens before population

The graph scatters candidate transforms, modifies their yaw/scale, moves them toward flatter ground, filters them with terrain masks, removes border candidates, and then chooses prefab shells. The shell contains spawn volumes and population FSMs, but its terrain placement does not itself instantiate its full enemy/merchant/loot batch.

Scatter density is initial candidates per square kilometre, not the final number of POIs. The lattice spacing formula is 1000 / sqrt(density). Later masking, slope movement, rarefying and borders change the accepted result.

Position stream Initial density Main processing Final shell selection
Small camps 0.05/km²; nominal lattice 4.472 km Yaw adjustment, slide toward ≤10° ground, safe border 40 m Small Common/Unusual split
Large camps/buildings 0.009/km²; nominal lattice 10.541 km Yaw adjustment, slide toward ≤10° ground, safe border 100 m Large Common/Uncommon split
Desert wrecks 0.1/km² Slide toward ≤5° ground; inverse dry, inverse redDesert, inverse small-camp-ground masks; safe border 40 m Wreck2, Wreck3, Wreck_5
Dry ambient sites 14/km² Rarefy radius 230 m; slide toward ≤15° ground; dry and inverse camp-ground masks; safe border 40 m Camp16, Wreck1, Wreck4, Wreck6, Wreck7, Wreck8, Cave2, Cave3
Main cave sites 10/km² Rarefy radius 930 m; slide toward ≤15° ground; dry and inverse camp-ground masks; safe border 100 m Main Cave Common/Uncommon split

The Slide operation has finite iterations. A stop-slope value guides movement; it is not a guaranteed final slope rejection rule. Rarefy compares two candidate radii: 230 m corresponds to 460 m pre-slide separation, and 930 m to 1860 m. Subsequent sliding can alter that spacing. SafeBorders removes candidates near each tile’s active edges to reduce problematic placement at seams.

Object masks sample a terrain value and compare it with a deterministic hash roll. They create probabilities, rather than a hard classification saying that every point belongs to exactly one biome. ObjectsOutput then chooses a prefab uniformly from the output’s list, using seeded coordinate noise, applies the final height/rotation/scale and instantiates or repositions the pool.

Every authored POI pool

All three category splits use Common weight 2 and alternate weight 1.5, giving nominal group shares 4/7 and 3/7. This is relative weighting after the earlier location filters. It is not a percentage of the entire map or a probability per metre driven.

Pool Variants Nominal share for each variant, conditional on an accepted position in this stream
Small Common Camp1, Camp2, Camp3, Camp5, Camp8, Camp9, Camp11, Camp16 ≈7.14%
Small Unusual Camp4, Camp6, Camp10, Camp12, Building1, Building7 ≈7.14%
Large Common Camp13, Camp15, Building2, Building3, Building_5 ≈11.43%
Large Uncommon Camp7, Camp14, Building4, Building6 ≈10.71%
Main Cave Common Cave1, Cave4 ≈28.57%
Main Cave Uncommon Cave5, Cave6, Cave_7 ≈14.29%
Desert wrecks Wreck2, Wreck3, Wreck_5 1/3 within that output
Dry ambient sites Camp16, Wreck1, Wreck4, Wreck6, Wreck7, Wreck8, Cave2, Cave3 1/8 within that output

The “Unusual” small group has fewer variants than the Common group, exactly balancing the nominal per-prefab share. Camp16 additionally appears in the dry ambient pool. Cave2 and Cave_3 use that ambient stream rather than the main cave split. Exact hash boundaries and later clipping mean the shares describe the authored selection rule, not a guaranteed histogram of a finite map.

There is no discovery-based removal of a shell variant from these lists. Discovering Camp10 once does not consume the Camp10 template. The existing runtime dump actually contains multiple Camp10 and Camp16 instances while those types are already known in the codex.

Sources: terrain review, graph Split531/564/589 and ObjectsOutput pools; encounter review, October 1 runtime camp observations.

Roads: links, routing, flattening and painting

There are two separate networks: small-camp/start roads and large-camp/building roads. The graph builds them from site candidates. Wreck and main-cave streams do not all feed a universal road planner.

The active graph has no standalone SplineOutput road-mesh node. A road is implemented through terrain height modification plus a painted terrain texture. The managed library contains other possible output types, but their existence does not make them active in this world.

Site positions
Floor→Nearby connections
Interlink→Terrain-aware route
Dijkstra→Smooth the spline
Relax / Optimize→Flatten + paint
Stamp / Stroke
  1. Project candidate positions onto heights. Small roads include the fixed start point and small-site candidates. Large roads use large-site candidates. These inputs are upstream of some SafeBorders filters, so a connection can be planned to a candidate that does not ultimately receive a shell.
  2. Create proximity links. Interlink uses three nearest-candidate attempts per point and a maximum-links cap of five. It suppresses duplicate/symmetric links and links with a mutual closer intermediary. This resembles a Gabriel proximity graph. The cap does not mean every site receives five roads.
  3. Route each link over terrain. Heights are downsampled to a 50 × 50 routing grid. An eight-neighbour Dijkstra implementation uses distance factor 0.5, elevation factor 20 and straightening factor 1, with maxElevation = 800 and endpoint welding enabled. Elevation and direction affect cost, so routes can curve around terrain. Failed routing can discard an edge; this is not proof of an always-connected global road network.
  4. Smooth and simplify. Relax uses blur 0.5 for 20 iterations. Optimize uses subdivision/split 3 and deviation 1 m to refine the spline and tangents.
  5. Stamp the height corridor. Both networks use Flatten stamping with flat range 10 m and blend range 100 m. These are influence ranges around a spline, not a literal total road width. The softened corridor merges into the surrounding height field.
  6. Flatten the destination pads. Small sites use radius 30 m and large sites radius 80 m. Other streams use 25 m for desert wrecks, 50 m for dry ambient sites and 70 m for main caves. Hardness is 0.72. Pad height comes from its sampled centre, not a universal sea-level platform.
  7. Paint the visible road. Each network has Stroke width parameter 1 and hardness 0.8, feeding its own road splat layer. Rasterization and approximately 4.88 m heightmap sampling affect the realized stripe. The visible stroke and the much broader terrain blending corridor are separate parameters.

The small road field is applied before the large road field. Site-ground texture strokes are separate from the height pads. That explains why the apparent road width, flat driving corridor and visible camp clearing need not match exactly.

Sources: terrain review, Interlink/Pathfinding/Relax/Optimize/Stamp/Stroke implementations and the two active graph chains.

Population: loot, NPCs, vehicles and merchants

The standard one-shot local spawner

Most local categories use an ItemSpawner FSM. “Item” here includes many NPCs and critters; it is not limited to pickup loot.

wait
  OnOff > 0? → spawned
  otherwise wait 1 second → trigger
trigger
  roll batch count; wait for Player entry
getItem / spawn
  choose prefab; create/register object; repeat batch
spawned
  set OnOff = 1; no normal exit

The one-second wait is initialization/restore time, not a replenishment cooldown. Re-enabling the standard FSM restarts its state machine, but ResetVariablesOnEnable = false preserves variables. A completed batch therefore starts at wait with OnOff = 1 and immediately remains consumed.

A POI can have separate spawners for ordinary enemies, additional enemies, critters, a boss, guards, general loot, unique loot, crates, merchants, merchandise, liquid merchandise, cars or trailers. Crossing a map-discovery trigger does not necessarily cross every spawn trigger. A camp can be discovered while some categories remain untriggered.

Choosing counts and prefabs

Counts are authored per child spawner and can be adjusted by another ItemNum FSM. RandomInt can include the maximum when inclusiveMax is enabled. For example, one inspected Coyote spawner rolls 3–4 and a critter spawner rolls 0–2. These are examples, not universal camp counts.

The 50 inspected ItemNum FSMs each make two constant assignments to their own spawner's min/max fields. They do not scale those counts with distance, boss defeats or a loot multiplier. Their overrides matter more than a copied child-prefab default: standard merchant stock uses 7–10, mechanic stock 7–8, and organic-mechanic stock 7–10 in these authored wrappers. Large physical loot batches include Building4/Building6 at 95–100 each, Camp14 at 85–90 and Camp7 at 55–60. These are per-spawner ranges, not totals including every guard, crate and unique-item batch. The evidence appendix retains the complete per-site count table.

Some batch FSMs create an object before checking the count. In the inspected critter loop, a rolled zero can still produce one creature. The serialized min/max pair should therefore not be read as a complete executable guarantee; the catalogue retains both ranges and state logic.

Ordinary loot uses weighted integer indices into the central item list. The audited example contains 272 choices with explicit relative weights, including very small rare-item weights. Authored enemy/critter spawners use their own EnemySpawn lists; ordinary cars use random choice from a CarSpawn list. Some unique-item spawners have only fixed entries. Selection is runtime randomness, separate from MapMagic’s layout seed.

For each created dynamic object, the common recipe is:

  1. Select a prefab and a spawn point, either the spawner transform or a child of its spawn_locations group.
  2. Create the object, commonly without a parent, and apply random yaw.
  3. Increment itemNameID, append its integer ID to the instance’s name, and register it in ArrayList_Items or ArrayList_Cars.
  4. Send the object’s initialization event, such as Randomize or ForBuy, when applicable.
  5. Continue until the batch is complete, then set the source spawner’s OnOff flag.

Object-level randomizers are a further layer: vehicles/parts can randomize condition and assembled configuration, containers can randomize liquids, and consumables/ammunition can randomize their state. The world spawner chooses the prefab; that prefab's own FSM decides its initial properties. Saving preserves surviving objects and their selected variables rather than rerolling the terrain seed to recover their condition.

The starting population has special rules

The starter car does not wait for the player to cross an ordinary camp trigger. After a 0.2-second wait it randomly selects from six variants: Poloska, Junker, PipeRat, Crossbreed, TinyTyrant and Halfbreed. It registers the vehicle and adds 15 to its randomized fuel value. Its starter engine follows the selected car index, choosing the compatible 594 cc or 1.2 L engine branch and applying starter condition/fluid bonuses. The starting item batch iterates a fixed 22-entry list rather than drawing 22 independent weighted loot choices. These automatic starter recipes are separate from later one-shot camp populations.

Poloska/PipeRat/TinyTyrant get a 594 cc engine and motorcycle radiator; Junker gets the 1.2 L engine and small radiator; Crossbreed/Halfbreed get the 594 cc engine and two motorcycle wheels. The helper adds to existing condition/liquid fields and attempts the appropriate cap-fluid changes; these are bonuses, not guaranteed final values on every part. Fixed supplies also receive their own additive initialization after Randomize.

The complete fixed starter supply list, in creation order

dogfoodcan; gaugeoiltemp; poloskaexhaust; Headlight; MotorOilCanSmall; smallwheel1; smallwheel2; WaterCanPlastic; poloskasteeringwheel1; poloskagearlever1; tincanlight; cassette80ssynthwave; bandage1; radiocar; a second smallwheel1; smallwheel3; RepairboxMedium; Toolbox; poloskaseatfronthomemade; GasolineCan; gauge_speedo; shiv.

These supplies stay the same across the six randomized chassis. The separate compatible engine/parts branch adapts to the car. The starter critter spawner is independent and follows its own Player-entry batch.

Merchants have three independent systems

System Owner/lifetime Practical consequence
Merchant NPC One-shot merchant spawner; registered dynamic Item Can be deactivated/deleted by item cleanup; deleting it does not reset its source flag
Goods the player can buy One-shot stock/liquid spawners; dynamic ForBuy objects Purchased or destroyed goods are not automatically replenished by a retained completed spawner
Goods the merchant wants from the player Static Sell_Items/ItemList generator Fresh construction/load can roll a new wanted list independently of the saved physical stock

Regular merchandise selection uses the active ArrayListGetRandomCurvedWeighted action. A legacy SelectRandomInt table in the inspected stock FSM is disabled, so its displayed weights do not define the active stock selection. The liquid stock FSM explicitly creates GasolineCan, DieselCan and WaterCanPlastic: three objects. Its min/max variables are not a substitute for inspecting those active creation states.

The standard wanted-list generator waits until Player is less than 500 m away, rolls 8–10 rows, draws candidates from ItemBuySellList using a weight curve, briefly instantiates each candidate to read its item name and sale value, writes the row data, and destroys the temporary object. It has no one-shot stock OnOff variable and no inspected Save/SaveGame transition. Duplicates are not conclusively excluded: the action’s decompiled selection method does not use its declared repeat field.

What “refreshes on save” actually means

The native save path activates registered dynamic Items before serialization. It does not explicitly restart the static Sell_Items/ItemList generator, and that generator is not registered in the dynamic item list. Therefore, the code does not support a guaranteed immediate wanted-list reroll from saving alone while standing near the same merchant.

A save followed by a fresh load reconstructs the static merchant site and generates its unsaved wanted list again when the distance condition is met. The merchant’s physical NPC and surviving physical stock follow object persistence and their separate spawn flags. A new wanted list does not imply newly stocked shelves or a respawned merchant.

Reactivating the same pooled static wanted-list FSM is another case: its arrays and counters survive, and no explicit clear/reset was found before generation. That may append or rewrite rows instead of performing a clean refresh. The fresh-instance load/recreation path is the supported reroll mechanism; a route-specific observed save-only change needs a runtime event trace.

Sources: persistence review, local batch FSMs, merchant-stock FSM, save-trigger trace and complete extracted spawner catalogue.

Bosses: sites, defeat flags and recurrence

Which boss belongs to which site?

The graph chooses the site shell from its weighted POI pool. The boss is then selected by that site’s child spawner. The seven named-boss spawners each choose their list’s first entry with weight 1 and spawn a single boss; they are not randomly choosing among all seven warlords.

Shell Boss Saved global death flag Placement pool
Camp_7 Buzzgut Boss_Buzzgut Large Uncommon
Camp_14 Duke Ironjaw Boss_Duke_Ironjaw Large Uncommon
Building_4 Black Juggernaut Boss_Black_Juggernaut Large Uncommon
Building_6 Professor Boss_Collage_Teacher Large Uncommon
Cave_5 Alpha Nightwalker Boss_Alpha_Nightwalker Main Cave Uncommon
Cave_6 Scorpion King Boss_Scorpion_King Main Cave Uncommon
Cave_7 Terror of the Night Boss_Terror_of_the_Night Main Cave Uncommon

No traveled-distance, boss-count, vehicle-speed or progression-tier prerequisite appears in those named spawners. Such rules exist in some encounter mods, but are not the vanilla named-site conditions.

Boss creation depends on entering the authored local spawn volume. The three main boss caves use approximately 3 m sphere triggers, Buzzgut’s trigger is approximately 5 m, and the building/Duke sites use boxes. These are encounter-room volumes, separate from the 500 m merchant-list distance or 5 km cleanup radius. Guards, regular enemies and room loot have independent spawners and can use other volumes/counts.

Discovery is not a boss death

Entering/discovering the site can update the site codex and map marker. The named boss's own Codex FSM is disabled in its living prefab and enabled by the death branch: merely seeing/fighting it is not the same persistent boss unlock. Killing the boss takes its Health FSM down that branch, disables its BossUI, creates/registers a dead body, sets the corresponding global Boolean to true and later removes the living actor. The player sheet uses those flags to show the killed portrait. Saving/restoring global FSM variables preserves the flags.

The player-sheet FSM's three-second refresh is just UI polling. It is not a three-second boss respawn timer. No universal timed reset of the seven death flags was found in the reviewed vanilla paths.

Starting New Game explicitly resets the seven defeat flags; loading an existing save restores that save's flags. Reusing a terrain seed does not automatically reuse the old character's boss progression.

If you discover or fight a boss and flee without killing it, its death flag stays false. That particular site's boss batch is nevertheless consumed once creation finishes. Other unused matching sites can still produce the same named boss, and a surviving original boss can remain alive until its own lifecycle or distance cleanup removes it. Seeing it once creates no global uniqueness lock.

The exact suppression rule and its exception

At the spawner’s initial wait state, it tests both its local completion state and the named global death flag:

OnOff > 0 OR corresponding Boss_* flag true
  → spawned / OnOff = 1 / no creation
otherwise, after the initialization wait
  → armed Player-entry trigger

The boss Boolean test is in wait, not continuously in the armed trigger state. If a second site has already left wait and armed its trigger before the boss is killed elsewhere, entering that second volume can still create that boss after the global flag has become true. This is a code-supported timing exception. An already living boss at another site is not automatically removed by setting the flag either.

Re-enabling the spawner restarts wait and checks the global flag again, while preserving local variables. Newly initialized/restored spawners normally suppress a defeated named boss. Consequently, “kill it once and no further instance can ever exist” is stronger than this implementation guarantees.

Situation Expected result from the inspected state logic
Discover site without entering boss volume Discovery can be saved; boss batch can remain untriggered
Complete boss batch, leave and return to retained site OnOff = 1 suppresses another batch, even if the original boss was distance-deleted
Kill boss, enter a newly initialized matching site Global death flag suppresses that boss spawner
Kill boss after another matching spawner is already armed That armed spawner can still produce it upon entry
Boss already alive elsewhere when flag becomes true The spawn check alone does not destroy the living instance
Load an older save before the defeat Restores the earlier global flag and older object state; this can make the boss available again

Guards, doors and unique loot

Boss suppression does not imply every guard or loot spawner is suppressed. Those have independent flags. The unique boss-room loot spawner checks its own OnOff and player trigger, rather than a generic boss-death requirement. Physical access can depend on the door machinery.

Site Independent attendant batch Active weighted choices
Cave_5 3–4 Nightwalker
Cave_6 9–10 Scorpion Small : Scorpion Big = 4:3
Cave_7 10–11 Bat
Camp_14 4–5 Lugnut, Scrud, Flexa, equal active weights
Building_4 6 Arachnid 0.2, Blast Zombie 0.1, Zombie Runner 0.5, Grimhound 0.2
Building_6 6 Arachnid 0.4, Teacher 0.15, Zombie Runner 0.3, Grimhound 0.3; normalized from total 1.15

Building_4's unique boss-room spawner iterates its complete 36-entry list, rather than drawing a single rare item. That list includes sanity pills, armor plates, Blastlance variants, grenades and ammunition. Its consumption flag remains independent from the named boss and guards. Other local spawners in these sites still use their own lists and triggers.

Building4 and Building6 door FSMs recheck their respective global death flags while waiting/closing and open when defeated. Duke’s site announces that a garage door outside has opened. Some cave door FSMs contain copied Duke-flag tests and null position targets; those serialized oddities should not be converted into a confident Alpha/Scorpion door-design claim.

Source: encounter review, resolved boss spawn lists, seven Health death branches and boss-door FSMs. The catalogue retains exact trigger dimensions and independent guard/loot definitions.

Discovery, visits, completion and saving

Three different kinds of remembered state

Record Scope What changes it Meaning
Codex Boolean, e.g. camp_10 Site type Type discovery trigger The character has discovered that archetype; saved under CODEX
Map-icon Visited.mapIcon Individual marker/site instance Player enters its marker trigger Marker appears visited; does not clear all population categories
Child spawner OnOff One local population category Batch finishes, or boss suppression branch That batch has already been used/suppressed
Global Boss_* Boolean Named boss progression Boss death branch That named boss has been defeated in this saved character state

The root site’s saveItemVar FSM snapshots selected child flags under a world-position-based key. For example, Camp10 records separate Critter, Merchant, MerchantItem, Enemy and MerchantLiquids values and restores them into the corresponding child FSMs on Load. Other sites store their own lists; boss sites include distinct boss/guard/unique-item categories. There is no universal single “visited means cleared” Boolean replacing this set.

The save sequence

  1. Activate registered Items so inactive objects can participate.
  2. Send SaveGame to the main save coordinator, NewGO_ArrayList, player roots, starter area, game manager and ID counter.
  3. Collect current dynamic objects/children and active static objects tagged SpawnerStatic.
  4. Send dynamic SaveGame and static Save events; static roots read their child variables into their own save FSM.
  5. Save registered car/item/sandstorm arrays and selected FSM/global variables; write the ES3 cache to disk.

The SaveAll action saves named variables, not the current PlayMaker state. A loaded one-shot batch remains consumed because OnOff is restored, not because a serialized program counter resumes in spawned.

The object arrays contain current surviving registered instances. A destroyed object is not merely an inactive object waiting in that array to be brought back. The cleanup system removes null references. Saving after destruction cannot recover the removed instance; loading a genuinely older save can restore its earlier population.

The load sequence and its reach

The coordinator restores the root terrain seed and MapMagic world offset, restores the sky controller's saved timeline with SetTimeline, enables/refreshes terrain, waits for generation, restores dynamic object snapshots and variables, finds currently active SpawnerStatic objects and sends Load to apply saved flags, then finishes loading. Saving captures that timeline with GetTimeline; world time is part of state rather than a newly randomized terrain input.

The active-only lookup is significant. Ordinary spawners do not contain a self-loading “read my saved position record whenever I become active” path. A site generated/enabled later outside that load sweep can therefore behave differently from a site active around the loaded player. This limits any claim that every historic camp everywhere is permanently consumed after a save.

Save-action inspector fields can show a literal editor-default filename even when overrideDefaultSettings = false. The actual ES3 settings come from the slot-selection settings in that case. The document uses the inspected save behavior rather than assuming every record is written to the displayed default file.

Sources: persistence review, `NewGO_ArrayList`, Camp_10 `saveItemVar`, `SaveLoadGame`, ES3 `SaveAll`/`LoadAll`/SettingsAction and `ArrayListFindGameObjectsByTag`.

Despawning, distance cleanup and the empty-camp case

The precise cleanup rules

Distances are 3D straight-line distance to Player, not odometer distance or road length. The sweeps wait in game time and walk registered lists; they are not instant callbacks at the exact moment the radius is crossed.

Object/list Condition Operation State consequence
ArrayList_Items, ordinary layer >1,000 m SetActive(false), during roughly five-second sweeps Preserves surviving instance/variables; below 1,000 m it can be enabled again
ArrayList_Items, layer 22 Layer test matches 22 Force active in activation sweep; skip item distance-deletion branch Protected from those item distance rules, not from every possible deletion path
ArrayList_Items, ordinary layer >5,000 m Destroy object during roughly ten-second sweeps Removes dynamic population; does not reset its source OnOff
ArrayList_Cars >5,000 m Destroy object and descendants No layer-22/ownership exemption in this car loop
ArrayList_Sandstorms >50,000 m Destroy object Separate storm lifetime
Registered Items or Cars World Y ≤−10,000 Destroy object Falling-object safety cleanup

The 1 km activation FSM walks Items, not the separate Cars list. A car registered only as a Car has no demonstrated 1 km sleep branch in this particular loop. Disabled kinematic actions in the item sleep FSM do not change Rigidbody kinematic state; the active behavior is GameObject activation.

Exactly 1,000 or 5,000 m does not trigger a new greater-than event. The interactive rule checker below is deliberately limited to these explicit list-cleanup branches; it does not predict terrain shell identity, faction AI or every object-specific death effect.

Inspect the distance rule

A concrete camp revisit

Assume the camp’s enemy trigger created its batch and set Enemy.OnOff to 1. The NPCs became independent registered dynamic objects. You travel sufficiently far from those NPCs that the 5 km cleanup destroys them. The cleanup does not know which local spawner originally produced them and does not set Enemy.OnOff back to zero.

If you return to the same retained camp shell, its enemy spawner is still consumed. It will not create a replacement batch. The camp can look empty even though its buildings, props and visited marker still exist. Loot, critters, merchants and vehicles follow their own category flags; an untriggered category can still spawn, and unrelated static decoration remains.

This is also why walking out and back after 1–4 km is different: surviving Items may simply be sleeping. Re-enabling them brings back the same instances. Some of their own FSMs restart on enable while preserving variables, so reactivation can have object-specific behavior, but it is not creation of a new camp batch.

“ItemRespawn” is not camp replenishment

The scene’s ItemRespawn FSM detects an existing layer-9 object touching its rescue trigger, moves it to Player position plus 10 m vertically, zeroes linear/angular velocity and waits 0.2 s. It does not instantiate a prefab or reset a camp. It is a fall-rescue mechanism, followed independently by the deeper Y≤−10,000 destruction safety net.

Source: persistence review, exact `DeleteFarAwayItems`, `DeactivateFarAwayItems`, `DeleteFallingItems`, `SaveGameActivateItems` and `ItemRespawn` actions.

Terrain streaming: retained, recycled or newly created

The terrain system uses tile coordinate neighbourhoods, while dynamic cleanup uses a distance sphere. A 5 km departure does not guarantee that the camp’s terrain tile or shell has been discarded.

Camera position is converted into MapMagic local space and divided by the 5,000 m tile size. Full/detail visibility follows tile indices. Because a camp and the player can be near different tile edges, their straight-line separation alone does not tell you whether its shell is still active, inactive but retained, or recycled.

Streaming state What happens to POI shells
Main 3 × 3 neighbourhood Full terrain and pooled POI Objects become active when generation is ready
Outside main, within draft 5 × 5 Draft terrain; POI Objects are deactivated, preserving their instances and FSM variables
Existing outer retention ring Already generated tile/data can be retained but hidden; this does not require fresh generation of an entire 7 × 7 area
Beyond retention Unpinned surplus tiles can be moved/reused for newly needed coordinates; leftovers can be destroyed
Pinned tile (0,0) Excluded from normal surplus recycling; its objects can still be inactive when far away

Moving a reusable tile clears its generated terrain products and readiness flags and regenerates its new coordinate. It does not immediately clear its object pool. Pool application then removes nulls, destroys excess instances, creates missing ones and moves surviving same-prefab instances by list index. It does not map each retained instance to its historical world coordinate or perform a general reset of its PlayMaker variables.

This creates three different revisit paths:

  1. Retained original shell. Same local OnOff variables remain. Distance-deleted dynamic categories can stay empty.
  2. Reused pooled shell. Geography is generated for the current coordinate, but a surviving prefab instance can retain state from its earlier use. You cannot assume OnOff = 0 simply because the tile moved.
  3. Fresh prefab shell. Authored flags start at their defaults. It can create another batch unless load-time restoration or the boss’s saved global flag suppresses it.

Revisiting a seeded coordinate reliably reconstructs the intended shell variant/transform, subject to the same graph recipe. It does not guarantee the same object identity or dynamic population. The active-only load restoration described earlier further changes which state reaches newly generated sites.

Floating origin and world coordinates

The actual scene component is NWH.Common.FloatingOrigin.FloatingOrigin on Player. At a main-camera distance threshold of 1,000 m from the current origin, it translates all root transforms in all loaded scenes by the camera position and shifts world-space particles, preserving numerical precision. It also temporarily handles rigidbody sleep and synchronizes transforms.

MapMagic moves with the scene and uses inverse-transform local coordinates, so the origin jump does not choose a new terrain seed or change the intended map. The save retains the MapMagic world position along with its seed. Straight-line player/object distances are invariant under the common translation. MapMagic’s own independent shift feature is disabled in this scene; an unrelated similarly named class in Assembly-CSharp is not the active origin component.

Source: terrain review, `TerrainTile.SwitchLod/Move`, `TileManager.Deploy`, `ObjectsPool` and active NWH floating-origin code.

Decoration, weather placement and runtime effects

The same graph produces more than major sites:

Generated content Placement rule
Rocks Initial 2/km²; seeded scale 0.3–5 and yaw; height offset −1 to −5; erosion-height contrast probability mask; rock8/7/5/4/2/1
Dry props Initial 50/km²; erosion-height selector and dry mask; scale 0.2–0.8; Dry4/Dry3/Dry2/Dry1
Grass Five main-detail outputs reading dry-layer Contrast10; densities 0.04, 0.004, 0.007, 0.004, 0.006; scene draw distance 100 m
Sandstorm shell Initial 0.0007/km²; nominal lattice ≈37.8 km; seed 938271; main-detail Sandstorm_1 output

There is no TreesOutput in this graph. A serialized tree-draw distance therefore does not prove procedural forest generation. Rock placement does not contain an additional road-rejection stream beyond its authored height mask. The sparse Sandstorm_1 placement is a graph location rule; moving storm behavior and tornado physics are runtime FSM behavior. Storm distance cleanup uses its own 50 km registered-list threshold.

The storm shell creates a moving hazard

Sandstorm_1 is a stationary one-shot shell. Its child named EnemySpawn_Sandstorm actually creates one SandStorm hazard, not a mutant group, after a one-second wait with no Player-entry or day/night gate. It registers that object in ArrayList_Sandstorms and marks its local category consumed. The root can save/restore that child flag.

The moving storm waits one second, aims toward Player once, then travels forward at a randomized 20–30 m/s. It does not continuously home toward the player in that Move FSM. On LoadVar it rerolls speed without the initial aiming action, so a load can change its speed while retaining the restored orientation.

Inside 2,500 m, the storm enables its player-dust particle emission and moves that particle object with Player; beyond 2,500 m it disables the emission. Exactly 2,500 m leaves the current comparison state unchanged. This is a presentation threshold, not a storm spawn or destruction radius. The prefab also contains tornado physics/damage children, making it a moving gameplay hazard rather than only a terrain visual.

Peaceful mode and disabled storms are cleanup rules

When enabled, the game manager's PeacefulMode waits five game-time seconds between sweeps, hides boss UI/stops boss music and destroys registered Items whose current layer is 10. The disable-storm setting similarly runs a five-second sweep over registered Sandstorms and destroys those on layer 2. These settings act after generation/spawning. They do not remove shell variants from the graph, reset the source OnOff, or restore deleted actors when switched off. A previously triggered category can therefore stay empty after the setting is disabled while its consumed state survives.

No day/night or difficulty spawn gate was found in the 219 reviewed static ItemSpawner definitions. One Wreck_7 branch chooses Mutant versus Carnivore with a random 0/1 roll instead of reading DayTime. This statement concerns content creation; darkness can still affect visuals and other NPC behavior.

World time, faction relations, sanity and object-specific effects are runtime gameplay state. They can change how a generated encounter behaves without changing its seeded location. For example, the inspected game-manager sanity-mutant spawn FSM exists but is disabled in the authored scene; its mere presence should not be presented as an always-running procedural encounter source. The full spawner catalogue includes storm and attack variants so these can be distinguished from the seven named-site bosses.

Sources: terrain review’s decoration streams and scene fields; source spawner catalogue; scene game-manager FSM enabled fields.

Revisit scenarios and practical implications

Scenario What returns What can remain absent or change
Discover a camp type, continue into unexplored terrain Other seeded camps of that type can appear Discovery does not remove the type from selection
Mark a site visited but avoid a child spawn volume Shell/visited marker Untriggered categories may still generate upon later entry
Leave sleeping ordinary Items at 2 km and return Surviving instances can reactivate They are not fresh randomized replacements
Leave completed camp population >5 km away, return to retained shell Static camp and its retained state Deleted categories stay consumed/empty
Travel far enough for terrain reuse/destruction Seeded shell layout on regeneration Dynamic content depends on reused/fresh shell flags and later load restoration
Save near consumed camp, then load near it Surviving saved dynamics and restored active-site flags Destroyed/bought stock is not intentionally replenished; wanted list can reroll
Load elsewhere and later generate a historical site Seeded shell variant Its position record is not automatically restored by ordinary spawner activation
Kill a named boss, initialize another matching site That site’s shell, guards/loot as independently allowed The named boss is normally suppressed by its saved global flag
Kill boss while another matching spawner is already armed Armed trigger can still create a boss Initial-only death test does not give universal uniqueness
Load an older pre-destruction/pre-defeat save Earlier object population/progression This is rollback, not a timed world refresh
Save beside the same active merchant without loading Native persistence and dynamic-item activation No confirmed immediate wanted-list reroll from that action alone

The implementation has separate concepts of “known,” “visited,” “spawned,” “dead,” “inactive,” “destroyed,” and “regenerated.” Treating any two as synonyms leads to wrong predictions. The safest code-backed gameplay statement is: a completed category does not replenish on return while its consumed state survives; terrain and save/load determine whether that state actually survives.

Mods, scope limits and verification

The installed startup log reviewed during this audit lists Apocaplayer, Apocasaver, Apocasetter and Apocaspawner. The repository contains additional encounter and cleanup mods. Repository presence is not evidence that a mod is active in the current play session.

Mod Relevant behavior Relationship to this document
Apocasaver Invokes the native save flow; adds autosave/naming/held-item handling Native activation/save side effects also occur on autosave; does not implement camp restocking
Apocaspawner Uses persistent item IDs and registers created items/cars Spawned objects can follow ordinary save and distance cleanup rules
Apocapatrol Own raider-car cleanup and persistence; its cleanup can protect ever-occupied cars Separate from the vanilla 5 km Cars loop; protection in one loop is not protection in all loops
Apocatremors Adds speed/travel/boss-count-gated ambushes and its own despawn distance Those thresholds are mod encounter criteria, not named-site vanilla generation
Gunplay / other NPC mods Can alter combat, boss health or AI Do not use those values to infer vanilla placement/recurrence

This review reads the installed binaries, scene/prefab fields and existing runtime inspector dumps. It did not launch a destructive gameplay experiment, alter saves, or deploy mod changes. Static graph and FSM claims are directly inspectable in the embedded evidence. Exact pooled-instance survival on a chosen route requires a controlled runtime observation.

The most useful follow-up verification cases would be a throwaway save tracking one camp’s child flags across >5 km travel, a much longer terrain-recycling route, loading nearby versus loading elsewhere, an already armed duplicate boss site, and a merchant save-only versus save-and-load comparison. Those experiments would confirm the live event timing and particular instance identity; they are not prerequisites for the explicit cleanup and spawn rules documented here.

Sources and exact installed-artifact hashes: evidence manifest. Detailed source references follow below.

Evidence & source notes

The reviews below retain exact object paths, state names, serialized fields, code methods and line references. The document describes this installed build. Runtime snapshots are dated 1 October 2026; they are observations, while packaged prefabs and graph values establish authored defaults.

Terrain and road review — source references and exact fields

Terrain, roads, seeded POI shells and terrain streaming

Evidence and scope

This is the installed game's actual MyDesert graph, not a description of optional MapMagic features. The packed sharedassets1.assets Graph at path ID 103111 and level1 MapMagicObject 11687 were parsed with regenerated Unity type trees and a manual reader; every raw byte was consumed: Graph 208,692/208,692, MapMagicObject 616/616. Graph has 140 nodes, all enabled, 668 serialized graph objects. See raw graph, decoded graph, named topology, and scene parameters. Numbers identifying nodes below are serializer indices in the decoded graph, not asset path IDs. Named topology has exactly one line per generator; its line numbers are cited below.

MapMagic is v2.1.12 (terrain-code/MapMagic.Core/MapMagicObject.cs:31). Its Graph.random is seeded coordinate noise, not the same thing as Unity's mutable gameplay random stream. Graph deserialization creates Noise(seed,32768) (terrain-code/MapMagic.Nodes/GraphSerializer200Beta.cs:84); subnode Noise(data.random,nodeSeed) shares the root permutation and uses a node-specific subSeed (terrain-code/Den/Den.Tools/Noise.cs:77). Coordinate/hash random results therefore reproduce the same graph outputs for a given world seed and coordinate. This reproduces shells, terrain and roads; it does not promise identical runtime loot/enemy rolls or persisted state.

Actual scene parameters

  • Tile size: 5,000 × 5,000 m. Full terrain resolution 1025 (1024 intervals, 4.8828125 m height sample spacing), margin16 samples. Draft65 (64 intervals, 78.125 m), margin2. Vertical height range600m. Main height uses TextureToHeightmap; draft SetHeights; no extra height interpolation. 500 generated objects per frame batch, max apply time3ms, multithreading enabled.
  • Generation centers on main camera, not separate tagged objects. Infinite generation enabled. Full detail/Objects active in mainRange1 (3×3 tiles); drafts in generateRange2 (5×5 tiles); retainMargin1 keeps already-existing tiles out through a further outer ring. Tile(0,0) is pinned, so it is never automatically recycled by the normal tile deployment queue, though its LOD/Objects can still be deactivated.
  • Terrain details draw100m; tree draw1000m (but no TreesOutput in this graph). Terrain materials use splatmaps. Height weld margin5 and splat weld2 make seams meet; generation includes border margins and welds height edges before applying terrain.
  • Starting position is explicitly (1696,0,2533), also used as a StartPos terrain lock: radius12m, transition6m, relativeHeight true, serialized guiHeight64.2371. MapMagic.Locks/Lock.cs:42 hooks runtime prepare/finalize: captures the existing terrain patch before regeneration, preserves it when writing output, and can offset preserved heights relative to newly generated terrain. This protects the authored starting patch; guiHeight is an editor field, not a promise of constant player altitude.

Sources: extracted/level1-11687-MapMagicObject.json (all fields), graph-summary.txt:52; TerrainTile.cs:485 gives main/draft data areas; TerrainTile.cs:607 generates, finalizes, reads/welds/writes edges, applies through main-thread coroutines. MapMagic.Core/MapMagicObject.cs:206 updates tile management each frame.

Height construction and terrain appearance

The base height pipeline is Perlin Noise3 → Curve18 → Terrace15 → Erosion8 → Levels138. Actual parameters:

  1. Perlin type2; node seed12345; intensity1.13; size5127m; detail0.45; turbulence0; offset(0,0). Runtime root world seed combines with this node seed. Noise evaluation is in world coordinates, including tile generation margins. Perlin/Linear/Simplex implementations run in NativePlugins rather than the managed C# loop; avoid inventing more detailed native math.
  2. Height curve remaps broad low areas and high plateaus. Control points (x,y): (0,0), (0.39568347,0.15107913), (0.64748204,0.46762589), (0.74820143,0.87769783), (0.86330932,0.96402878), (1,1). Tangents and 256-value LUT are in decoded graph node18.
  3. Terrace has 8 levels; uniformity0.25; steepness0.36; seed12345.
  4. Erosion3 iterations; durability0.62; erosion1; sediment0.45; fluidity5; relax0. Erosion native steps order heights, create torrents, erode, transfer/settle sediment. Draft calculation reduces3 iterations to1 (Erosion200.cs:78 onward).
  5. Levels: input min0.11/max0.991, gamma1.307, output0–1.

The base is then modified by both roads and the POI terrain pads. Actual dependency order:

base → small roads124 → small pads102 → large roads512 → large pads507 → desert wreck pads293 → dry wreck/cave pads361 → cave pads452 → HeightOutput11.

Sources: named topology graph-summary.txt:1,2,4,5,24; :17,22,59,60,66,79,124–126; node138 parameters decoded JSON. Height output is both Main/Draft. HeightOutput200.cs:60 shows normalized heights scaled to terrain size.y; TerrainTile.cs:607 shows workflow.

There is one desert graph, no Whittaker/BiomesSet graph. Terms dry, redDesert, Cliff etc are texture/control masks, not a separate biome selection system. Nine texture slots:

Slot Input mask
Desert Background layer (filled1 before blending)
dry Convex cavity of small-road/small-pad modified height, intensity20, spread100
redDesert Contrast of that height: brightness0, contrast3
stone_ground Concave cavity: intensity5, spread20
Cliff Slope25–90°, transition range30°
road Small road Stroke
building Small POI position Stroke radius20m
building2 Large POI position Stroke radius70m

Texture layers are blended in the authored order, then splat channels normalized at finalize time (BaseTexturesOutput.cs:60, TexturesOutput200.cs:134). Later road and building layers take priority in blending. The same generated dry layer product is reused as a probability mask for other decoration/POIs, so “dry ground” is terrain-derived, not an independent biome map. Sources graph-summary.txt:6–8,25,26,34,40,113,121.

Authoring quirk: Matrix Mask nodes403 (DryGrassyMask) and415 (DesertMask) both have A=dry and B=small modified height, but their third mask input is unconnected. MatrixGenerators/Mask200.cs:48–55 returns A when mask is null; therefore both effectively return dry despite opposite invert flags. Their names must not be mistaken for implemented climate logic. Object mask288 inverts this result to select non-dry wreck positions. Its later mask422 also inverts redDesert and387 inverts small camp ground.

How POI locations and prefab variants are chosen

The generation graph creates site transforms first, chooses a prefab shell, then the shell's PlayMaker FSMs handle discovery/contents/progression. It does not directly choose bosses or check discovered-camp history. “POE” has no dedicated generator type in this graph; shell names are Camp_, Cave_, Wreck_, Building_.

Scatter200.Scatter calculates lattice spacing = 1000 / sqrt(density); density is initial candidate density per square kilometre. It expands the processing rectangle by a cell, scatters seeded positions, relaxes them, and later clips objects to active tile bounds. These densities are not guaranteed final POI counts: slope sliding, masks, borders and rarefying remove/move candidates. Sources ObjectsGenerators/Scatter200.cs:33–63; Den/Den.Tools/PositionMatrix.cs:68, :87, :276.

Most placement streams randomize yaw, then slide candidates down terrain towards flatter areas (blur2; node iterations100, internally resolution-scaled; small/large stopSlope10°). This is not a strict final slope rejection: Slide moves while over threshold and has finite iterations (SlideGenerator200.cs:44–110). SafeBorders throws away candidates within40m or100m of active tile edges (SafeBorders218.cs:24–55). Object masks compare sampled mask to a deterministic hash roll, not simple “allowed/disallowed biome” labels (ObjectsGenerators/Mask200.cs:86). ObjectsOutput selects each accepted transform's prefab by root+node noise(hash), uniformly within that output's prefab list (ObjectsOutput.cs:220–235). It samples final height, applies rotation/scale, converts position to tile-local, then instantiates/repositions the appropriate pool.

Stream Authored density/seed Processing and output
Small camps 0.05/km², seed12344; nominal lattice4.472km Adjust yaw → Slide stop10/move0.5 → safe40 → Split531
Large camps 0.009/km², seed91271; nominal lattice10.541km Adjust yaw → Slide stop10/move0.5 → safe100 → Split564
Desert wrecks 0.1/km², seed25149 Adjust → Slide stop5/move10 → inverse dry → inverse redDesert → inverse small camp ground → safe40 → uniform Wreck2, Wreck3, Wreck_5
Dry wreck/cave sites 14/km², seed98854 Rarefy distance230 → Adjust → Slide stop15/move0.7 → dry mask → inverse small camp ground → safe40 → uniform Camp16, Wreck1, Wreck4, Wreck6, Wreck7, Wreck8, Cave2, Cave3

Rarefy's distance is radius, so self spacing rejection tests num + num:230 yields pre-slide candidate separation460m;930 yields1860m. Those are not guaranteed final distances because the later Slide can move points (Rarefy200.cs:104–112). Road generation in detail

Two separate networks: small camp/start roads and large camp/building roads. There is no active SplineOutput node, separate road mesh output, road entity or all-world path planning pass in MyDesert. The traversable surface is terrain modified by a spline-height Stamp and painted with a terrain-layer Stroke. A generic SplineOutput class exists in the DLL but is unused by this graph.

For each network:

  1. Ground the site transforms with Floor (small relative, large absolute). Small uses combined start+small sites; large uses large candidates before safe borders. Connections can involve candidate sites which are later removed by SafeBorders from actual shell instantiation.
  2. Interlink: Gabriel-like proximity graph, iterations3 nearest-candidate attempts per position; maxLinks5; withinTile=false; clamp=Full. It excludes duplicate/symmetric links and links when a mutual closer intermediary exists. “Max5” is an upper cap; with3 nearest tries it does not mean five roads per camp. It constructs line splines. Border/margin processing permits local network connections across tile context; avoid promising global connectivity.
  3. Pathfinding downsamples heights to50×50, routes each edge using FixedListPathfinding.FindPathDijkstra over eight neighbours. Parameters distance0.5, elevation20, straighten1, maxElevation800, weldEndpoints true. It weights length, elevation and direction, so routes bend around height variation instead of straight lines. maxIterations1,000,000 is stored on Pathfinding200 but the actual fixed-list implementation's own loop is bounded by Manhattan distance×2 and reconstruction1000; don't call it a million-iteration guarantee. Failed paths return null, so no guarantee every candidate link survives.
  4. Relax blur0.5, iterations20; Optimize subdivides3 then adjusts tangents, reduces deviations1m, and updates spline.
  5. Stamp Flatten algorithm, flatRange10m, blendRange100m, detailRange32/detail1/falloff1 (detail settings don't add detail because algorithmFlatten). It paints a centreline height and spreads/pads it into a target height field; blends that with source terrain to flatten road corridor and soften edges. Here range is radial influence; don't label “10m” as total road width.
  6. Height around site centres gets flattened after road stamping:30m radius for small sites and80m large. Pad hardness0.72, sizeFactor1, noiseFalloff true/amount2; noiseSize2 small,10 large. Other sites pads25m desert wreck,50m dry sites,70m main caves. A flattened pad uses existing sampled height at its centre, not always sea level (Flatten200.cs:47, :98).
  7. Separate Stroke produces road splat weights, width parameter1 and hardness0.8. Width is a spread-distance parameter converted by terrain pixel size, not necessarily a precisely2m visual stripe; centreline raster antialiasing and ~4.88m terrain sampling affect the realized appearance. Painted road's influence and100m blend corridor are separate parameters.

Sources graph-summary.txt:12–22,48,111–125; Interlink200.cs:66,114; Pathfinding200.cs:56,101; FixedListPathfinding.cs:29; Pathfinding.cs:26 (CalcWeight); Relax200.cs:29; Optimize200.cs:24; SplinesGenerators/Stamp200.cs:54,82; SplinesGenerators/Stroke200.cs:27,59.

What terrain streaming means for revisits

The5km dynamic-object cleanup radius and terrain tile streaming are different systems. Terrain does not destroy a Camp shell just because the player is5,001m from it. Actual5,000m tile membership and tile indices determine full/detail visibility. Tile distances are axis-priority (max(dx,dz)+min(dx,dz)/(max+1)), then integer-truncated by TerrainTile, so mainRange1 is a square3×3 neighbourhood, not a5km sphere. Centre camera position is transformed into MapMagic local coordinates before floor(tile/5000), so floating-origin changes do not create new terrain coordinates. Sources Den/Den.Tools/Coord.cs:498, TileManager.cs:121–170, TerrainTile.cs:253.

  • Inside main3×3: pooled POI Objects active once full terrain ready.
  • Outside main but inside draft5×5: switch to draft terrain; Objects GameObject.SetActive(false), preserving its children/FSM instance data. Reactivating returns same shell instance if tile not recycled. This is not respawn or deletion.
  • Already-existing outer ring out through generateRange2+retainMargin1 (tile-axis distance3): retain tile object/data to reduce churn, but hide far terrain and pooled objects. This ring is retention of existing tiles, not a fresh7×7 generation requirement.
  • Outside retained rectangle: surplus tiles enter a reuse queue. allowMove=true recycles them to newly needed coordinates; leftover surplus tiles get Destroy. Pinned(0,0) never enters surplus queue.

When a tile is moved, TerrainTile.Move stops generation, clears main/draft generated products, resets ready flags, disables active terrain and sets new transform/coord; then generates graph at the new coordinate. It does not destroy/clear objectsPool at Move time. ObjectsOutput later repositions the pool: null instances removed, excess instances destroyed, insufficient counts instantiated, surviving same-prefab instances moved by list index. It does not match pool instance identity to a world coordinate and it does not run a generic ResetFSM. All authored outputs have allowReposition=true and instantiateClones=false; in this build Pool.Reposition itself does not branch on allowReposition anyway.

Consequences:

  • Leaving5km and returning while site shell is retained can yield same shell with its one-time OnOff/spawn flags unchanged even though independently spawned enemies/loot were destroyed by their own cleanup.
  • Regenerating an old coordinate reproduces the same seeded shell type and transform, not necessarily the same in-memory shell. A freshly instantiated prefab starts from authored state unless a save load restores it. A reused same-prefab shell can retain old state after relocation; do not claim fresh local contents merely because terrain generated again.
  • “It respawns” and “it is permanently empty” are both overbroad answers for terrain alone. The answer depends on retained/reused/fresh shell identity, its per-object spawn flags, global progression and whether save/load restores those variables. Discovery markers/history are separate from physical shell lifetime.

Sources MapMagic.Terrains/TerrainTile.cs:253 SwitchLod, :299 Objects setactive, :383 Move, :418 Dist, :449 Remove; Den/Den.Tools/TileManager.cs:206 Deploy; Den/Den.Tools/ObjectsPool.cs:73 ClearNulls, :84 ClampCount, :98 AppendCount, :112 MoveItems, :138 Reposition, :155 RepositionRoutine, :226 SetPrototypes, :304 RepositionRoutine. Static analysis proves these operations; a route-specific guarantee about which pooled instance survives requires runtime observation.

Save/load and floating origin

New-game seed acquisition (menu scene verified)

The main menu level0 is now extracted and all37 PlayMaker FSMs decoded. The world seed is the player's numeric text input, not a freshly randomized number on New Game. Seed GameObject50 has InputField393 with authored m_Text = "12345", m_ContentType = 2 (IntegerNumber), m_CharacterValidation = 1 (Integer), m_CharacterLimit = 9, editable, and no persistent OnEndEdit/OnValueChanged callbacks. Its GetSeed FSM395 has one getseed state, which runs UiInputFieldGetTextAsInt every frame and stores its result in local seed.

The NewGame FSM350 starts idle. In clicked, it copies Seed.GetSeed.seed to its own seed, disables relevant menu controls, resets starting statistics and money15, and asynchronously loads Game with DontDestroyOnLoad true. When loading emits next, it enters disableCanvas, resets the seven Boss_* death flags false, finds Game's SaveLoadGame object, and sets that FSM's local seed to the copied integer. SaveLoadGame's existing setSeed step then assigns this integer to Graph.random.Seed before terrain refresh. Keeping12345 gives the same terrain recipe for repeated new games; entering another valid integer changes it. No RandomInt/RandomFloat or other random-seed action exists in the37 decoded menu FSMs.

UiInputFieldGetTextAsInt.DoGetTextValue uses int.TryParse(inputField.text, out _value) and assigns _value unconditionally. Invalid/empty/out-of-range text therefore yields 0, rather than a random or default fallback. The menu has no isInt/isNotInt events wired and no explicit invalid-seed guard. Character validation restricts ordinary edits, but clearing the field is still materially different from leaving12345.

Evidence: menu-fsm.txt:80 NewGame350, :86 seed copy, :99 LoadLevel, :100–110 disableCanvas/global resets/seed transfer; :166–168 GetSeed395; extracted/menu-seed-inputfield.json (436/436 bytes consumed); extracted/menu-decoded-fsm.json (37 FSMs and raw variables); terrain-code/game/HutongGames.PlayMaker.Actions.UiInputFieldGetTextAsInt.decompiled.cs:67 DoGetTextValue. Level0 was extracted read-only from data.unity3d; no game/save changes.

Saving, reconstruction and coordinate translation

The scene initially serializes MapMagic disabled. SaveLoadGame sets Graph.random.Seed before enabling and Refresh, waits for IsGenerating=false. Saving reads root seed and MapMagic world position into FSM variables; loading LoadAll restores them, applies root seed and world position, then enables/Refresh. So a save preserves a regeneration recipe plus world offset; it does not serialize the complete infinite terrain heightmap.

Scene uses NWH.Common.FloatingOrigin.FloatingOrigin, not the unrelated FloatingOrigin class in Assembly-CSharp. Its actual distanceThreshold1000m, attached to Player; it checks main camera magnitude, invokes BeforeJump (temporarily sleep rigidbodies), subtracts camera position from every root transform in all loaded scenes, shifts world-space particle positions, then restores sleep thresholds and Physics.SyncTransforms. MapMagic root moves together with player/scene, and tile manager uses InverseTransformPoint to recover local coordinates. This maintains precision without changing seed/local world layout. MapMagic's own shift flag=false.

Sources extracted/level1-13495-FloatingOrigin.json; terrain-code/game/NWH.Common.FloatingOrigin.FloatingOrigin.decompiled.cs:64 LateUpdate and :78 Jump; old runtime fsm_detail.txt:59729–60033 (SaveLoadGame, SaveGame, LoadGame, setSeed, generateTerrain/2). Avoid citing the unused Assembly-CSharp FloatingOrigin implementation for actual shifts.

Encounters and boss review — source references and exact fields

Encounter/discovery review (vanilla)

Evidence reviewed: installed game managed assembly, decoded static Unity prefabs, and the inspector snapshots fsm_dump.txt / fsm_detail.txt dated October 1, 2026. Runtime values in the snapshot are observations of that save, not defaults. Early snapshot observations below are resolved by the final decoded specification later in this review.

Confirmed distinctions

  1. A landmark type being discovered is different from an individual landmark being visited. The game manager Codex owns booleans such as camp_1 … camp_16, cave_1 … cave_7, building_1 … building_7, wreck_1 … wreck_8, poi_1, poi_2 (detail lines 593–722). Its global event SaveGame saves all local Codex FSM variables under CODEX; LoadVar restores them (detail 723–775). This is a catalog of discovered types. A site's map icon separately owns Visited.mapIcon and its own position-based save FSM (example Cave7: dump 25205–25239; Camp10 dump 7828–7861). These records do not encode “all instances of Camp_10 are consumed.”

  2. The same camp archetype repeats. The October 1 snapshot has Camp10 in Tile 0,0 and Tile 2,1, and Camp16 in Tile 0,0; Tile 4,2; Tile 4,3 (dump 5878, 7620, 6322, 23866, 26366). The game manager already has camp_10=True while multiple Camp_10 instances exist. A catalog unlock is therefore not a uniqueness restriction on future world layout.

  3. Boss flags record deaths, not discovery. The seven global flags are Boss_Alpha_Nightwalker, Boss_Black_Juggernaut, Boss_Buzzgut, Boss_Duke_Ironjaw, Boss_Collage_Teacher (Professor), Boss_Scorpion_King, Boss_Terror_of_the_Night (dump 46116 and 46122–46127). The player sheet's warlord FSM tests its corresponding global flag; true switches the portrait to a killed/dead texture (detail 38823–39011). Its three-second wait is an UI polling interval, not a boss respawn cooldown. SaveLoadGame saves/restores global FSM variables under key global (detail 59778–59888), so these death flags persist across saves.

  4. Site content has separate consumed flags. Cave_7 owns OnOff_Critter, OnOff_Enemy, OnOff_Item, OnOff_Enemy_2, OnOff_Enemy_3, OnOff_Enemy_Boss, OnOff_ItemUnique (dump 24901–24921). Each child spawner tracks OnOff and enters a terminal spawned state with SetIntValue. This is separate from map visit/Codex discovery and separate from a named boss's global death flag. Root save/load copies child flags via GetFsmInt/SetFsmInt. The exact bindings matter; do not assume every variable listed is necessarily saved unless the action fields confirm it.

Named boss site observed in runtime

Cave_7(Clone)/EnemySpawn_Wild_Boss has one boss quota (numberEnd=1 observed), an ItemSpawner FSM with RandomInt → proximity/trigger → SelectRandomInt → ArrayListGet → CreateObject, and an extra BoolTest in its initial wait state (dump 24980–25009). Its local variables include Boss_Duke_Ironjaw; the variable's name alone does not identify the actual tested global or selected boss prefab. Static action parameter decoding is required before assigning this site to Duke or describing a boss recurrence condition.

Cave_7/EnemySpawn_Wild_boss_bodyguards is a separate spawner, with sampled numberEnd 10 and no boss BoolTest in its initial wait (dump 25010–25038). Two regular wild-enemy spawners, a unique-item spawner, random-item spawner, and crate spawner are separate again (dump 24937–24979 and 25039–25190). A named boss being suppressed does not itself prove guards/loot are suppressed.

Random selection semantics

Installed Assembly-CSharp.dll action HutongGames.PlayMaker.Actions.SelectRandomInt selects one entry using ActionHelpers.GetRandomWeightedIndex(weights) and returns the matching integer from ints. Weights are relative, so 0.5 is half the probability mass of 1; raw weights are not percentages. See research/encounter-code/HutongGames.PlayMaker.Actions.SelectRandomInt.cs.

RandomInt uses Unity Random.Range(min,max+1) when inclusiveMax=true, otherwise Unity Random.Range(min,max) (upper bound excluded). Its default noRepeat prevents the same consecutive result only for non-inclusive ranges wider than one; this applies to consecutive draws in that action's lifetime, not persistent per-world uniqueness. See research/encounter-code/HutongGames.PlayMaker.Actions.RandomInt.cs.

Mod distinction

Apocatremors calculates its own car-speed/travel-kilometers/boss-kill thresholds for mod-driven encounters (Apocatremors/Catalog.cs 19–28, 139–173). These are not evidence of vanilla world POI/boss gates. Its comment identifying the seven global boss flags as kills agrees with the vanilla player-sheet FSM (Catalog.cs 179–187). Gunplay changes human boss health (Duke base 1500; Buzzgut 600), not vanilla boss placement (gunplay/src/Bosses.cs 7–24). Keep these separate from the vanilla design document.

Final decoded boss-site specification

The installed sharedassets1.assets prefab data is now decoded into extracted/decoded-fsm.json. encounter-fsm.txt is a readable action dump; extracted/boss-site-table.json resolves each boss spawner's EnemySpawn ArrayList proxy. Static asset IDs below are stable references to the reviewed components.

These shapes are room-entry volumes, with local centers and sizes; they are not a “distance from POI center” test. Spawn and trigger positions can differ. Rotation, parent scale, and world placement affect the final world coordinates.

Every named boss spawner chooses integer index [0] with weight [1], resolves the single associated boss prefab from its local EnemySpawn proxy, and sets the count range to min=1/max=1/inclusive=true. Consequently the world generator picks which site shell, and that shell determines the named boss. There is no second weighted lottery between all seven bosses at room entry. No travel distance, day/night, previously discovered camp, or minimum defeated-boss count is tested in these seven spawn FSMs. The uncommon shell selection in the MapMagic graph makes these encounters uncommon, not a boss progression ladder.

Exact boss recurrence state machine

  1. On initialization or re-enable, start in wait. If OnOff>0, transition back to spawned. If the corresponding global death flag is true, also transition back to spawned. spawned writes OnOff=1 and stops. If neither gate blocks, wait one scaled second, then enter trigger.
  2. trigger chooses a quota of one and waits for a collider tagged Player to enter (TriggerEvent.trigger=0, OnTriggerEnter). It then draws index zero, creates the boss, registers it in NewGO_ArrayList/ArrayList_Items, appends the global item ID to its name, and finishes with OnOff=1.
  3. The global death flag is only checked in wait. Once a spawner has reached trigger, it does not recheck the flag. Another copy of the same site's room that was already armed before a boss was killed can still create that boss later. Newly initialized/re-enabled copies do honor the death flag. This explains a repeat after a kill without inventing a respawn timer. Multiple live copies are also possible before the first kill because spawning/seeing one does not set the global death flag.
  4. RestartOnEnable=1 and ResetVariablesOnEnable=0 on all seven named boss spawners. Re-enabling an existing consumed spawner restarts its wait, retains OnOff=1, and skips creating another boss. Its saved root binding can restore the consumed flag after a save/load reconstruction. Seeing the same shell elsewhere does not mean it shares the previous site's consumed flag.
  5. A boss killed state is global to that boss type; the spawner-consumed state is local to that site. A boss merely encountered/fled from leaves its death flag false, but that site still has already-spawned OnOff=1. If the spawned object is later destroyed by distance cleanup, the consumed spawner does not replenish it on a retained-instance revisit. Pooling/reconstruction after tile removal is a separate lifecycle question covered by the persistence/terrain review.

The observed Cave_7 local variable named Boss_Duke_Ironjaw in fsm_dump.txt is a leftover local variable. The actual BoolTest parameter binds Boss_Terror_of_the_Night. Do not infer actual gates from unused local variable names.

Death and boss discovery

Each named boss's Health FSM tests Health<1 every frame, enters its death spawn state, disables its BossUI, enables its previously disabled Codex FSM, creates/registers a dead-body prefab, and writes its corresponding Boss_* global to true. The later drop/trophy flow destroys the live actor. Exact Health IDs: Black 104864, Buzzgut 107440, Duke 107683, Scorpion 110322, Terror 110512, Alpha 111848, Professor 112533. All seven Codex FSMs are disabled in their live prefab and enabled in this death branch. Thus the boss Codex unlock is tied to death in these prefabs; merely seeing/fighting a boss is not the same persistent event.

SaveLoadGame saves/restores global variables, so the death flags persist. No timer anywhere in these named spawner/death flows clears those flags. The 3-second player-sheet poll, 1-second spawner initialization delay, and 8-second garage-door message are not respawn cooldowns.

Boss attendants and room loot are independent

Each following attendant spawner tests its own OnOff but has no Boss_* death gate. All listed ranges use inclusive bounds:
